L’accès aux polices d’assurance difficil: Access to insurance policies difficult on Indigenous reserves
« Ça rentre dans la catégorie de la disc: “That falls under the category of illegal discrimination. File a complaint with the Human Rights Commission.”
Qu’on soit député ou simple citoyen, l’a: Whether they are a member of the National Assembly or an ordinary citizen, getting an insurance policy seems to be a challenge for Indigenous people. In 2018, Alexis Wawanoloath wanted to insure his car. He was living on a reserve at the time. When he gave his address to the insurer, Industrielle Alliance, he was reportedly told: “Oh, that’s on a reserve; we don’t insure there.”
Un membre de la communauté atikamekw de: A member of the Atikamekw community of Manawan, who preferred to remain anonymous, says he pays twice as much for car insurance because he lives on a reserve.
« Dès que les compagnies d’assurance voi: “As soon as insurance companies see that the mailing address is on a reserve, they raise their price. We all have the same problem with that. We pay a lot for our insurance; it costs me $2,000 a year for a Ford 150. I did some research; one of my kids lives in an urban area, and when I used his address, my insurance cost me $1,000 less.”
Daniel G. Nolett, directeur général de l: Daniel G. Nolett, director general of the Abenaki community of Odanak, confirms that insurance costs more for those who live on a reserve.
« Parfois, on se fait appeler par des co: “Sometimes companies call us, and then when we give the postal code, they answer: ‘Oops! That’s in a First Nations community; sorry, we don’t cover that.’ They don’t want to insure if it’s a First Nations community, urban or remote, because they’re afraid of vandalism… So some companies make no distinction and simply cover no one on reserves. It’s a problem we’ve raised on several occasions. It’s harder for some people to find insurance, and premiums are often higher too.”
<strong>Redlining : le lieu de résidence: Redlining: place of residence as grounds for discrimination?
Wawanoloath, ancien député du Parti québ: Wawanoloath, a former Parti québécois member of the National Assembly, sees this as <l1>redlining,</l1> a discriminatory practice that consists of refusing or limiting loans to people living in certain geographic areas.
Michel Morin, professeur de droit à l’Un: Michel Morin, a law professor at the Université de Montréal, explains that the principle of non-discrimination applies to people, not to place of residence. So it is conceivable, though surprising, that in some areas insurers may have refused to insure certain property. Trying to understand the reasons for refusing car insurance, the law professor suggested that vandalism potentially present in certain communities could be the cause of a refusal.
« S’il y a eu beaucoup de vandalisme con: “If there has been a lot of vandalism against cars, that can be a legitimate reason, but the insurer has to be able to prove it if a complaint is filed against it with the Commission des droits de la personne et des droits de la jeunesse (CDPDJ), because if the real reason is that the insurance application comes from an Indigenous person, that is not acceptable; it’s discriminatory. The insurer has to base its decision on objective criteria. There really has to be very, very convincing data, and not just isolated incidents.”
À l’époque, Alexis Wawanoloath est étudi: At the time, Alexis Wawanoloath was a law student. He told one of his professors, Daniel Proulx, who teaches human rights law, about his situation. “That falls under the category of illegal discrimination. File a complaint with the Human Rights Commission,” he told him. The student followed his professor’s advice and filed a complaint with the CDPDJ. Ten months after the complaint was filed, the Commission offered Mr. Wawanoloath mediation.
Ce dernier demande à ce que la médiation: He asked that the mediation be held on his reserve. His request was refused. The mediation finally took place at the Commission’s offices. Mr. Wawanoloath went to the mediation alone, while the insurance company’s vice-president and its lawyer attended by videoconference. Although he is a law student, he felt wronged during the mediation. “It’s a very, very unfair process, it gets you nowhere, the mediator knows nothing about systemic racism,” he says.
Alors qu’Alexis Wawanoloath termine le b: While Alexis Wawanoloath was finishing bar school and looking after his pregnant wife and two children in the middle of the pandemic, the Commission threatened to close his file if he did not provide certain information about his current insurance. Mr. Wawanoloath does not understand why he is being asked for information that has nothing to do with his complaint.
« Mon dossier comporte une plainte de ra: “My file contains a complaint of systemic racism for things I experienced at the hands of Industrielle Alliance. The investigation therefore concerns that company’s actions toward me and toward Indigenous people living on reserves in Quebec, whom it refuses to insure. I fail to see how my insurance file with another company is relevant to moving such an investigation forward.”
En ne transmettant pas assez vite ces in: Because he did not provide this information quickly enough, the former MNA saw his complaint file closed by the Commission on August 25, 2020, three months after an investigator was assigned to it. He considered the decision hasty and suspicious. He then began asking questions about the investigator in charge of his file at the CDPDJ.
« Ce monsieur avait aussi une entreprise: “This man also had a business that offered services to insurance companies. So he’s a claims specialist who handled my file like a claims specialist,” he says. The former MNA then demanded that an independent investigator handle his case. He also asked that an independent investigation be opened into the investigator’s apparent conflict of interest.
Enfin, il a souhaité qu’une introspectio: Finally, he wanted an internal review of systemic racism within the CDPDJ.
Questionnée à ce sujet, la Commission a: Asked about this, the Commission said it was not aware of its investigator’s professional activities before he joined the Commission. But it defended itself by saying that he had no longer worked as an insurance specialist since that time. A new investigator was assigned to Mr. Wawanoloath’s file.
À propos de la fermeture de son dossier,: Regarding the closing of his file, the Commission told the former MNA that he had to file a new complaint with the Commission or go to the courts of common law to seek redress.
« La réponse de la Commission, je l’ai t: “I found the Commission’s response astonishing and disrespectful. The Commission should treat the people it is supposed to defend with more consideration.” In the end, the initial complaint file was reopened, and a new investigator was assigned to it.
Wawanoloath a procédé à des recherches s: Wawanoloath researched the complaints filed with the Commission and found only 17 from Indigenous people since 2001. He considers that number far too low given systemic racism in Canada.
« Est-ce que vous avez les bonnes approc: “Do you have the right approaches with communities? Do you have Indigenous employees who understand the sensitivities of these communities?” Mr. Wawanoloath asks the Commission. “Seventeen cases in almost 20 years! When we know Indigenous people are victims of discrimination!”

« Il faudrait être assisté d’un avocat p: “You’d need to have a lawyer to deal with the Commission. I’m going to have to take my file and go defend it myself before a court of common law. I have a law degree, I’ve been a member of the National Assembly, and I’m discouraged,” he says. Beyond the changes made within the insurance company targeted by his complaint, he is asking the Commission to review how it handles Indigenous people’s files.
Fo Niemi, co-fondateur du Centre de rech: Fo Niemi, co-founder of the Centre de recherche-action sur les relations raciales (CRARR), is following Mr. Wawanoloath’s case closely. “There is discrimination in the sale of insurance policies on Indigenous reserves, and it’s something we’ve been hearing about for a long time. But we don’t know how widespread it is in the insurance industry. The other question is how Mr. Wawanoloath was treated when he filed his complaint.”
Le spécialiste de l’accès à l’égalité de: The specialist in minority equal access in Quebec knows the Commission des droits de la personne well, since CRARR often deals with it. “There have been fairly long, sometimes inexplicable delays in the handling of complaints since the start of the pandemic. Since March, there has been a lot of pressure from investigators, who are trying to speed up the processing of complaints. We wonder whether this acceleration is meant to carry out investigations more swiftly or to get complaints dropped so as to close the more complex files.”
Selon Fo Niemi, la Commission manquerait: According to Fo Niemi, the Commission lacks training on systemic racism, even though the very purpose of the organization is to investigate situations of discrimination and exploitation under the Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms. He condemns the Commission, which, in his view, lacks the skills needed to handle sensitive cases like Mr. Wawanoloath’s, which is harmful to Indigenous communities. “With this case, the Commission has lost all its credibility with Indigenous communities,” says the CRARR co-founder. The Commission declined to answer our questions – it “does not publicly comment on complaint files, since they are confidential.”
Elle a néanmoins tenu à nous préciser qu: It nevertheless wanted to tell us that its “investigative work is carried out rigorously, impartially and without conflict of interest.”
Nous avons aussi voulu connaître les pol: We also wanted to learn about Industrielle Alliance’s policies toward Indigenous people and its conditions for granting car insurance policies, particularly in Alexis Wawanoloath’s case.
L’Industrielle Alliance n’a pas répondu: Industrielle Alliance did not answer our questions and declined our interview requests. It only stated that it had chosen to be present in certain regions of Quebec and not in others. Beyond the changes he would like to see made at the insurance company in question, Mr. Wawanoloath is asking that changes be made at the Commission in how it handles Indigenous files.
